content_html_sanitized:
Posted March 9, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: This is not a surprise, but it is good that the Swiss really are moving along with their promised reforms.

It will be interesting to see if any of the major DEAland prohibitionist propaganda outlets, such as the New York Times or the Washington Pravda report this. There has been an almost complete blackout on the recent move by Belgium to decriminalize possession and personal cultivation.

Last November, the Swiss Federal Commission for Drug Issues – made up of prominent people from the financial, medical, academic and law-enforcement worlds issued a report saying that cannabis policy must reflect prevailing moral values and attitudes to civil liberties. The report concluded that using criminal law to dictate the behavior of an individual user " is repugnant to the fundamental values of a legal system founded on personal liberties, and is therefore illegitimate ".

The Swiss Parliament is due to act on this proposal by June, which could have an impact on the Canadian government, which will be reviewing its marijuana laws at that time, but it is certain to influence events in Germany and perhaps other Swiss neighbors as well.

In fact, the Dutch will actually be under pressure to regularize cultivation.)
See
Dutch Parliament Surprises Its Own Government -- Votes to " Legalize " Cultivation of Marijuana – By One Vote.

Swiss clear the way for cannabis legalisation

BERNE, March 9 (Reuters) - The Swiss government on Friday endorsed a draft law that would legalise the consumption of marijuana and hashish and allow a limited number of " dope shops. "
(MarijuanaNews note: The use of the word " dope " is offensive, but it may not be as pejorative in the European context. Reuters has a very mixed record of reporting on cannabis issues.)

The bill submitted to parliament seeks to bring Swiss law into line with the reality that one in four people aged 15-24 regularly gets high in the Alpine state, according to a poll commissioned last month by the Swiss government.
(MarijuanaNews note:The survey conducted by the private Swiss Institute for Alcohol and Drug Problems showed that 54 percent of the Swiss favored a " softening of penalties " for smoking, possessing and selling cannabis. In the survey of 1,600 people aged 15-74, more than a quarter said they had smoked a joint at least once in their life, with the figure rising to 50 percent among teen-agers and young adults. They also reported that around 87,000 out of seven million Swiss smoke every day.)

" Decriminalising the consumption of cannabis and the acts leading up to this takes account of social reality and unburdens police and the courts, " the government said in a statement.

The cabinet agreed in principle in October to legalise dope smoking.

It has now recommended that police be allowed to turn a blind eye to people growing and trading small amounts of soft drugs, arguing that this will make it easier to differentiate between small and large-scale production and export of drugs.
(MarijuanaNews note: This means there will be a de facto – not formal – legalization, which sidesteps the various " drug " treaties.)

" A certain number of shops could be tolerated as well as the growing of hemp and the production of cannabis products, to the extent that conditions laid down by government decree are fulfilled, " it said.
(MarijuanaNews note: This was excerpted from a Reuters copyrighted story, so we know that every newspaper in DEAland will have seen this story. Few will choose to run it.)
